summary: Audit a sample of already-applied drill rewrites against the originals they replaced: one adversarial substance verifier per batch of ten, told the stored key, reporting only defects it can quote
logs: auditing 200 applied rewrites in 20 batches of 10
audited 200 drills in 20/20 batches: 6 fatal, 27 style

fatal.detail: The rewrite deleted the only statement that the expected price move is adverse, and the stem never says which side the order is. Arrival price (the key, B) is correct only for a buyer: if the manager is selling, the expected buying pressure into the close is favorable and C, 'a closing auction order', becomes the defensible choice. Rationale B still argues from a fact the stem no longer supplies - 'An arrival price algorithm is most appropriate for trading this order because the portfolio manager has adverse price expectations' - so the input the question turns on now exists only in the answer explanation. Fixable by restoring the adversity, e.g. by saying the manager has a moderate-size buy order.
fatal.quote_before: For a portfolio manager expecting short-term buying pressure by other participants into the market close (adverse price expectations), the most appropriate algorithm for a moderate-size order in a liquid stock is most likely:
fatal.quote_after: A portfolio manager with a moderate-size order in a liquid stock expects short-term buying pressure from other participants into the market close. The most appropriate algorithm for the order is most likely:

fatal.detail: Shortening option B deleted the modal qualifier that made it false, and the reframed stem no longer anchors the item to the model-fee disclosure, so B is now a true statement competing with the key. Before, B was false only because it asserted exclusivity: 'must be computed using each client's actual negotiated fee, never a model fee.' After, B is the bare phrase 'each client's actual negotiated fee', which under GIPS is a permitted basis for net-of-fees returns. The old stem named the method under test ('Net-of-fees calculation using model management fee most likely:') and option A carried the Exhibit 8 disclosure; the new stem ('The fee deducted to compute net-of-fees composite returns is most likely:') is generic, so nothing in the item rules out actual fees. The after-rationale for B argues only non-obligation, not falsity ('a firm is not obliged to compute net-of-fees composite returns from each client's actual negotiated fee'), which cannot eliminate it. Key A ('a model fee based on the highest applicable fee schedule') is still true but no longer uniquely best — the item is double-keyed between A and B.
fatal.quote_before: Net-of-fees returns must be computed using each client's actual negotiated fee, never a model fee.

fatal.detail: The stem was left exactly as it was - "For the 2.5% rebalancing, Thompson most likely uses:" - while every piece of context was stripped out of the options. Before, the key option itself carried the answer and its reasoning ('Based on relative expected costs, Thompson would likely decide to rebalance the portfolio in the cash markets...' plus 'Larger size implies longer time horizon which favors cash market'), and distractor C supplied the corridor premise ('because the drift falls within QUINCO's tolerance corridors'). Shortening the options to 'Derivatives.' / 'The cash market.' / 'No rebalancing.' was right under rules 1-5, but it removed the only inputs in the item. What is left names an unintroduced person (Thompson) and an unintroduced institution (QUINCO, now only in the rationale), gives no portfolio, no relative cost estimates, no desired speed of implementation, and no smaller rebalancing to contrast 2.5% against - so nothing in the item supports the 'larger size implies a longer horizon' inference the keyed rationale depends on. Rule 9 cases like this were supposed to be reframed (inline the data or ask the conceptual question); this one was shortened instead, which converted a giveaway item into an unanswerable one. The key has not moved and B is still the curriculum-correct answer, but it is no longer reachable from the item.
fatal.quote_before: stem: "For the 2.5% rebalancing, Thompson most likely uses:" / option B: "Cash markets — 'Based on relative expected costs, Thompson would likely decide to rebalance the portfolio in the cash markets by reallocating between international developed equity and fixed-income investment managers.' Larger size implies longer time horizon which favors cash market." / option C: "For the 2.5% scenario, no rebalancing is undertaken because the drift falls within QUINCO's tolerance corridors."
fatal.quote_after: stem: "For the 2.5% rebalancing, Thompson most likely uses:" / option B: "The cash market." / option C: "No rebalancing."

fatal.detail: Shortening the distractor deleted the word that made it false. In "before" the option was "Nasdaq only." — the exclusivity claim (Nasdaq and no one else / Nasdaq as the sole remaining provider) is what the rationale rebuts. In "after" it is the bare noun "Nasdaq.", so under the rewritten stem ("A major global equity index provider ... is most likely:") the option asserts only that Nasdaq is a major global equity index provider — which is true: Nasdaq publishes and licenses the Nasdaq-100, Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq OMX index families. The item is now double-keyed: C is as defensible as the stored key B. The "after" rationale for C concedes the point ("Nasdaq operates the Nasdaq family of indexes") and can only dismiss it by appealing to membership in "the five major equity index providers" — a list the stem no longer mentions. Note this also leaves no stated reason to exclude A once the closed-set framing is gone, since NYSE publishes the NYSE Composite.

The stem changed from a closed-set recall question into an open real-world classification question, and the key is only correct under the framing that was removed. "Before" bound the item to the reading's enumeration — four named providers plus the one missing member of a list of exactly five — so there was exactly one right answer. "After" asks which firm is "a major global equity index provider," which is a question about the world, not about the reading's list, and admits more than one answer. The three rationales in "after" all still argue from "the five major equity index providers," a set the learner can no longer see in the stem, so the item is also no longer answerable from itself: nothing in the question tells the candidate that only five firms count or that exchange operators are excluded. This is the stem-side half of the same break; the rewrite needed to keep the five-provider framing (e.g. "The reading's five major equity index providers include CRSP, FTSE Russell, Morningstar, MSCI, and most likely:") to keep B the unique answer.
fatal.quote_before: "stem": "The reading identifies five major equity index providers. These include CRSP, FTSE Russell, Morningstar, MSCI, and most likely:"
fatal.quote_after: "stem": "A major global equity index provider, alongside CRSP, FTSE Russell, Morningstar, and MSCI, is most likely:"

fatal.detail: Option A lost the exclusivity qualifier that made it false, and the loss is what breaks the item. Before, A read "Adebayo violated only Standard I(C) by overstating expected returns to the hedge fund partners." The word "only" is the whole defect in that option: it concedes a misstatement but denies the suitability failure, so it is eliminable without the learner having to decide whether I(C) is also implicated. After, A is bare "Misrepresentation." against key B "Suitability." Stripped of "only", A is defensibly true on the facts the rewrite moved into the stem: Adebayo "assures them that NI is committed to providing investors with high rates of return" while the stem itself establishes that NI's mandate requires "both a beneficial socioeconomic impact and a positive expected investment return" and that "investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor." An assurance of high rates of return that NI is not in fact committed to deliver is an untrue statement about the strategy, and assurances of performance are squarely Standard I(C) territory. The item now has two defensible answers under a single-best-answer "most likely a violation of" stem; B is the standard the case solution names, but A is no longer wrong, only less central. The after rationale for A concedes the collision rather than closing it, arguing only that the suitability reading is the better one ("a bare misstatement under Standard I(C)" is called not the point rather than untrue) and it still describes an option that no longer says what it describes: it answers "Adebayo overstated expected returns to the hedge fund partners," wording that exists only in the before option. Fix is to restore the eliminating detail in the option itself rather than in the rationale.
fatal.quote_before: Adebayo violated only Standard I(C) by overstating expected returns to the hedge fund partners.

style.detail: The reframe did not merely supply the inputs, it supplied the answer's two components already attributed, so the item reduces to adding two numbers printed in the stem. LOS h is about decomposing a roll-down return into its credit-spread and benchmark-curve parts; that decomposition is now pre-done for the learner. The spec permits move 3 ('Keep the arithmetic but supply every input. Only when the computation itself is the point of the LOS'), but the inputs here would be the yields, spreads and coupons from which the attribution is derived, not the finished attribution. The key (C) is still correct, unique and unambiguous, and A ($506,500) and B ($0) are still both false, so the item is not broken, only emptied. Note also that the correct option is now literally the sum of two figures the stem states, which is the kind of structural giveaway the house style elsewhere works to remove.
style.quote_before: In Example 26 (AUD static credit curve, roll 15y to 14.5y over 6 months on AUD 50M face), rolling-down total gain is $506,500. The portion attributable to credit spread roll-down is most likely:
style.quote_after: Of that price appreciation, $217,250 is attributable to the credit spread narrowing from 0.85% to 0.815%, and $75,000 of the coupon income is attributable to the credit spread rather than to the government curve. The portion of the total gain attributable to credit spread roll-down is closest to:

style.detail: The reframed stem contradicts itself on its face: it tells the learner that credit spreads are expected to be stable over the horizon, then two sentences later states that the credit spread narrowed from 0.85% to 0.815%. The 'before' wording ('AUD static credit curve') was precise in a way the rewrite lost: a static spread CURVE means each maturity point keeps its spread while the bond itself rolls down to a lower point on an upward-sloping curve, which is exactly where the 0.035% narrowing (half the 0.07% total YTM decline, per the rationale) comes from. Rendered as 'stable ... credit spreads', it reads as an assertion that the spread did not move. All the arithmetic is internally consistent ($344,000 + $162,500 = $506,500; $217,250 + $75,000 = $292,250; $506,500 - $292,250 = $214,250 as rationale B states), so this is wording, not a numeric defect, but a careful learner is told the spread both did and did not change.
style.quote_before: In Example 26 (AUD static credit curve, roll 15y to 14.5y over 6 months on AUD 50M face)
style.quote_after: expects stable benchmark yields and credit spreads over the next six months and rolls the position down to 14.5 years

style.detail: The three options are no longer parallel, and the odd shape is the key. A and B are predicates about both structures ("identical for the two structures", "absent in both structures"), while C alone describes one leg of one structure. The rewritten stem asks for a comparison ("the vega and theta obtained from buying a call rather than from writing a put"), and C does not make a comparison at all — it states only the call side. The key is still unambiguously correct (long vega 0.018, theta -0.018/day) and A and B are both still false per their rationales, so nothing is broken; but the shape rule 7 warns about (the one option of a different grammatical kind names the answer) now fires, where in "before" the giveaway was length and capitals instead.
style.quote_before: C. Long call + short stock: the investor is LONG VEGA (from purchasing call) and exposed to negative theta (time decay hurts).
style.quote_after: A. identical for the two structures. / B. absent in both structures. / C. long vega and negative theta with the call.

style.detail: Distractor B changed its subject. In "before" the claim was about the FCM's own role — that it clears only for itself rather than acting for a client. In "after" the claim is about the investor dispensing with an FCM altogether. Both readings are false, and the "after" rationale ("The FCM is an essential intermediary, not an arrangement the investor can dispense with by clearing its own trades") does describe the option as it now reads, so the item is not broken and the key (C, clearing house member trading on the investor's behalf) is untouched. But the letter no longer carries the same claim it carried before: the predicate moved from the FCM to the investor, which is a substantive re-voicing rather than a shortening.
style.quote_before: Self-clearing only.
style.quote_after: A self-clearing investor acting without an intermediary.

style.detail: The rewrite removed the only facts inside the item that identified R-SWF's approach. The stem is carried over unchanged and names a case entity the learner cannot open ("For the Sunnyland airport, R-SWF's currency risk management is most likely based on:"), supplying no data at all. In "before", key option B itself carried the identifying evidence (70% of revenue as USD airport charges via IATA), so a learner could see in the item which mechanism was being described. In "after" all three options are bare mechanism labels and the 70% IATA figure and the $300 million USD-denominated debt appear only in the rationale, which the learner reads after committing. The key is still correct and both distractors are still false, so this is not fatal — a learner who studied this case reading can answer it — but the item's inputs now sit entirely outside the question, which is the condition rule 9 exists to prevent. Flagged at style rather than fatal because the stem's dependence on the case pre-dates the rewrite and because moving figures out of options into rationales is what rules 1 and 3 ask for; the correct fix here was a reframe or inlining the currency facts in the stem, not deletion.
style.quote_before: Structural mitigation: 70% revenue as USD airport charges (via IATA).
style.quote_after: structural alignment of US dollar revenues with US dollar debt.

style.detail: The rewritten rationale for the keyed option B introduces two specific volatility figures that appear nowhere in "before" (neither "13.2" nor "12.5" occurs anywhere in the before block for this item). The before rationale supported only the unquantified comparative "modestly higher short-term volatility"; the after version asserts exact values the source material in "before" does not supply, so a learner is taught numbers the item cannot vouch for. The rest of the item is sound: the stem now inlines the 70% maintenance probability, so 30% (key B) follows as its complement, 35% is correctly attributed to the current allocation, and 50% is correctly rejected.
style.quote_before: The Monte Carlo analysis shows proposed SAA better preserves purchasing power over long horizon despite modestly higher short-term volatility.
style.quote_after: The proposed allocation therefore better preserves purchasing power over the long horizon despite modestly higher short-term volatility, 13.2% against 12.5%.

style.detail: Option A no longer makes the claim it made before. Before it denied that any example links attribution design to the investment process (a claim about the source text); after it asserts a normative proposition about attribution design itself. Rationale A was replaced to match - before: 'the stock-picker illustration exists precisely to make the process-alignment point'; after: 'Connecting the attribution design to the manager's investment process is precisely the requirement.' The new claim is still false and the key in B ('sector effects for a benchmark-agnostic stock picker are a byproduct') is still correct and clearly best, so this is not fatal; it is a substituted distractor rather than a shortened one, which the reframe of this item (the old stem pointed at an example the learner cannot open) makes defensible but should be recorded.
style.quote_before: No example connects attribution design to the manager's investment process.
style.quote_after: attribution design need not connect to the manager's investment process.

style.detail: The key's claim was narrowed. 'Different from benchmark' is a difference in exposure - the first term of the decomposition the rationale still quotes, 'R_A = Σ(β_pk − β_bk) × F_k + (α + ε)' - whereas 'rewarded risks the benchmark lacks' implies β_bk = 0 for the tilted factors, a special case. Rationale B still describes the broader claim ('long-term exposures to rewarded risks that differ from those of the benchmark'), so option and rationale no longer say the same thing. The narrowed statement remains a true source of active return and B is still clearly best against A (matching benchmark weights) and C (minimizing turnover), so not fatal.
style.quote_before: (1) strategically adjusting active weights to create long-term exposures to rewarded risks different from benchmark.
style.quote_after: tilting active weights toward rewarded risks the benchmark lacks.

style.detail: Option C is not parallel with A and B, which are standard titles, and it does not read into the stem: 'The team's practice is most likely a violation of: ... C. No Standard.' The 'no violation' sense survives and the reasoning was correctly moved into rationale C ('Discretionary authority settles whether the team may trade without consulting the client; it says nothing about the order in which clients are served'), so the key in B ('Fair Dealing.') is unaffected. Something like 'no standard, given the team's discretionary authority' or a third standard title would restore the shape.
style.quote_before: There is no violation because discretionary authority allows the team to trade at any time.
style.quote_after: No Standard.

style.detail: Option B lost the qualifier that made it false, and its rationale no longer defeats it as it now reads. Before, B asserted that the conduct was "fully addressed by Standard VI(A)" - i.e. that this is a disclosure problem and disclosure would cure it - and the before rationale killed exactly that: "Disclosure would not cure it; trading ahead of client transactions is a PRIORITY violation under VI(B)." After, B is only the bare standard name "Disclosure of Conflicts.", answering the stem "Corrales's personal purchase is most likely a violation of:". The after rationale then half-concedes it: "Standard VI(A) would require Corrales to disclose a personal stake that could impair his objectivity, but disclosure would not cure what he did here" - that sentence says VI(A) imposes a requirement, but never says VI(A) was not violated, so it no longer shows the option wrong. Not fatal: the stem states no fact about disclosure, so a VI(A) violation is not established on the facts given, and the SIC case solution's Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions remains the clearly best answer in the keyed slot A - the item is not double-keyed. The rationale for B should be restored to a reason B is wrong (priority, not disclosure, is the standard breached by trading ahead of a known client transaction) rather than a reason VI(A) applies.
style.quote_before: Corrales's conduct is fully addressed by Standard VI(A) as an undisclosed conflict of interest. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.
style.quote_after: Disclosure of Conflicts.

style.detail: The distractor lost the assertion that made it false, and its rationale now rebuts a claim the option no longer makes. Before, C asserted that the terms are costless: 'Partnership liquidity terms carry no cost to investors because lockups are compensated by fee discounts' — false on the 'no cost' clause. After, it asserts only that discounts are granted, which is defensible in isolation; it survives as a distractor only because a fee discount is not a disadvantage, which is already the reason B ('protection from panic selling') is wrong, so the item's two distractors now fail for the same reason instead of two. The 'after' rationale still answers the deleted clause: 'No automatic fee compensation accompanies partnership liquidity terms, and even where fees are negotiated lower the cost of the terms remains real'. Not fatal: A, 'lost flexibility to adjust allocations and meet unexpected needs', is still the unique correct answer to the stem 'Of the effects of partnership liquidity terms, the disadvantage to investors is most likely:'.
style.quote_before: Partnership liquidity terms carry no cost to investors because lockups are compensated by fee discounts.
style.quote_after: fee discounts granted in exchange for the lockup.

style.detail: Distractor B lost the absolute qualifier that made it flatly false. 'Always harmful' is false on its face, because a single protective instance refutes it. 'harmful to market quality' is a bare normative claim about circuit breakers, which is a genuinely contested empirical question rather than something the item can simply treat as wrong. The matching rationale still argues the old claim ('They have a protective role rather than a harmful one'), i.e. it rebuts 'always harmful' rather than the weaker statement B now makes. Not fatal: the stem asks what trade halts are, and keyed C ('triggered when prices move too quickly') is the direct curriculum statement and remains uniquely best, so the item is not double-keyed. But B now reads as defensible rather than wrong, which is exactly the qualifier loss this pass was supposed to avoid.
style.quote_before: "Always harmful."
style.quote_after: "harmful to market quality."

style.detail: The reframe generalized the stem away from the named case (R-SWF/ABC) to 'a sovereign wealth fund managing exit challenges in its illiquid private holdings' - plural, and with no specific position introduced - but all three options were re-voiced with a definite reference to a singular 'the stake' that the stem never supplies: 'A secondary sale of the stake', 'A contractual put of the stake back to the founder'. 'the founder' is likewise a definite reference to someone the generalized stem never mentions. The old options were anchored to ABC, so the definite article had a referent; now it has none. The key is unaffected and A is still clearly best, so this is wording, not substance: either the stem names a single founder-held stake or the options should read 'a stake' and 'the company's founder'. Related, the keyed rationale still leans on case figures the generalized stem does not introduce ('the full 35% stake was sold to an international beverage company for $27 million'), which is permitted in a rationale but sits oddly under a stem that is no longer about that company.
style.quote_before: "Secondary sales (as done with ABC's $27M sale to a strategic buyer)." / "Exercising contractual put options back to ABC's founder."
style.quote_after: "A secondary sale of the stake to a strategic buyer." / "A contractual put of the stake back to the founder."

style.detail: Option C no longer reads as a continuation of the rewritten stem. The stem is now "A disadvantage of holdings-based style analysis (HBSA) is most likely:", so slotting C gives "A disadvantage of HBSA is most likely no disadvantage at all." The before version was a standalone sentence and read coherently. The claim and its falsity are unchanged, the key (A) is unaffected, and the rationale still describes C correctly, so this is wording only.
style.quote_before: Holdings-based style analysis has no disadvantages because it uses actual positions.
style.quote_after: no disadvantage at all.

style.detail: Shortening distractor B deleted the prohibition that made it false. Before, B asserted that audience sophistication "may not be considered" and that "all clients must receive identical detail" - a flatly false statement of what III(D) permits. After, B asserts only the practice of giving every client the same detail, which Standard III(D) does not forbid: a uniform presentation can still be fair, accurate, and complete, and tailoring is a recommended practice rather than a requirement. Not fatal, because the stem asks what "most appropriately meets her obligations" and A (tailoring) is still unambiguously the best of the three, but B is now merely less appropriate instead of wrong. The after rationale for B shows the drift: it argues only that different audiences "can properly receive different levels of detail", never that uniform detail breaches the standard, so it no longer explains why the option as now worded is incorrect.
style.quote_before: Audience sophistication may not be considered, since all clients must receive identical detail.
style.quote_after: providing every client the same level of detail.

style.detail: The rewritten stem dropped the only mention of Standard III(D) (before: "GIPS compliance recommendation under III(D) most likely:"), but the key option still points at it with the bare phrase "the standard", which now has no antecedent anywhere in the item - the stem's only named standards are the GIPS standards, so "the best method of meeting the standard" reads circularly as GIPS compliance being the best way to meet GIPS. The learner can still pick B by elimination (A and C are clearly false), so this is a readability defect, not a broken item; naming Standard III(D) in the stem would restore the referent.
style.quote_before: For members and candidates who are showing performance history of assets they manage, compliance with GIPS standards is the BEST METHOD to meet their obligations under Standard III(D).
style.quote_after: Recommended as the best method of meeting the standard.

style.detail: The key option's proposition shifted slightly in compression: before it said aggregate duration cannot capture how a portfolio RESPONDS TO non-parallel shifts (a statement about measuring price sensitivity); after it says aggregate duration cannot capture the shifts themselves, which reads as a claim about describing curve movements rather than portfolio exposure. Both readings are true and B is still clearly the best of the three (A is false, C is false), so the key does not move and the item is not broken; the after rationale still carries the original "responds to" framing and the KRD comparison reasoning, which is why the drift is recoverable rather than fatal.
style.quote_before: Aggregate portfolio duration cannot capture how a portfolio responds to non-parallel yield curve shifts.
style.quote_after: aggregate duration cannot capture non-parallel yield curve shifts.

style.detail: The reframed stem ends in a qualifier the spec does not list. Rule 8 requires the stem to close with a CFA qualifier ("is most likely", "is closest to", "best describes", "is least likely", "is most appropriate"); "the most likely accurate statement is that" buries "most likely" inside a noun phrase. The reframe itself is legitimate and an improvement - the before stem presupposed the answer by asserting that KRD analysis provides more information - and the item remains answerable from itself, so this is phrasing only.
style.quote_before: The reading emphasizes that KRD analysis provides more information than aggregate duration comparison alone because most likely:
style.quote_after: Regarding the information content of aggregate portfolio duration and key rate durations, the most likely accurate statement is that:

style.detail: The rewrite deleted the universal quantifier that made distractor B false. Before, B was an absolute claim; after, it is a bare statement that is in fact satisfied by one of the institutions the item's own 'after' rationale cites: rationale A reads 'The Future Fund of Australia targets CPI plus 4% to 5%' and rationale B itself concedes 'The consumer price index is only one of the metrics in use'. Read as a general claim about institutional investors the option is still wrong (GIC uses G3 inflation, some US endowments use HEPI), and key A, 'defined to suit the institution.', is still unambiguously the best of the three against the curriculum sentence, so the item is not mis-keyed or double-keyed. Recording it only because dropping the qualifier is the pattern this audit watches for; no change to the key or the stem is needed.
style.quote_before: "B": "Always CPI."
style.quote_after: "B": "defined as the consumer price index."

style.detail: The rewritten stem dropped "measurement error", which is the subject every option and all three rationales are organised around (A: "free of measurement error"; C: "insensitive to the duration measure chosen"; rationale B: "that approximation is a source of measurement error even for Type I cash flows"). In doing so it also re-predicated the key's claim of the wrong quantity: in "before" the weighted average of individual durations approximates "asset portfolio duration" (years), whereas the "after" stem plus option B asserts that asset BPV (a currency amount per basis point) "is... approximated by a weighted average of component durations". The key is not at risk, since A and C remain flatly false against the reading and B is the only true option, so the item is still answerable and correctly keyed; it simply reads less precisely than the version it replaced.
style.quote_before: Asset BPV measurement error even for Type I cash flows most likely: / B. "In practice common to approximate asset portfolio duration using weighted average of individual durations for component bonds."
style.quote_after: In the classic immunization strategy for Type I cash flows, asset BPV is most likely: / B. "approximated by a weighted average of component durations."

style.detail: The rewrite keeps the curriculum's claim that a long risk reversal aligns with a bullish view plus a declining-volatility outlook, but invents a justification for it that is wrong. "before" states the conclusion bare: "combined position aligned with bullish view + declining volatility outlook". "after" appends a causal clause: "The combined position therefore aligns with a bullish view on the underlying together with an outlook for declining implied volatility, since both legs benefit as the premium paid away falls." Both legs do not benefit from falling implied volatility: the long call leg is long vega and loses value as implied volatility declines; only the short put leg gains. The key and all three options are unaffected, so the item is still correctly keyed and answerable — this is a learner-facing inaccuracy introduced into the rationale, not a broken question. (A secondary wrinkle in the same item's A rationale, "Pairing the bearish leg combination with the long risk reversal reverses the position: the long risk reversal is the bullish side of the pair", is merely garbled rather than wrong.)
style.quote_before: combined position aligned with bullish view + declining volatility outlook
style.quote_after: since both legs benefit as the premium paid away falls

style.detail: Flagged for completeness, not as a rewrite defect: the stem is byte-identical in "before" and "after" ("QUINCO's active risk budget for the TAA program is most likely:"), so the rewrite neither introduced nor fixed this. The item cannot be answered from itself — nothing in the stem says who QUINCO is, what its prior budget was, or what its Board decided, and the answer is a recall of a specific case-study fact (the Board raised the budget from 100 bps to 250 bps with up to 150 bps earmarked for TAA). This is exactly the spec's rule 9 failure, and the reframe ladder was available (inline the data, or ask the conceptual question). Also minor within option A: "before" reads "with up to 150 bps of the 250 bps available for TAA program use" and "after" drops the qualifier to "with 150 bps of that usable for TAA", turning a ceiling into a flat figure; the A rationale still says "up to 150 bps", and the key does not move, so this is not fatal.
style.quote_before: QUINCO's active risk budget for the TAA program is most likely:
style.quote_after: QUINCO's active risk budget for the TAA program is most likely:

style.detail: The reframed stem now hands the learner the answer. It asserts both the direction and the localization that were the only things the three options discriminated on: 'the market prices slightly greater credit risk for BMS only at the 5-year and near-30-year maturities'. That sentence by itself kills B (which puts the premium on LLY) and C (which makes the premium parallel across all maturities), so A is pickable without any knowledge of spread curves. The old stem supplied no such cue: it only said the two issuers were 'both A2/A+ rated' and asked what their spread curves look like. Key A is still correct and both distractors are still false, so this is not fatal, but the item no longer tests the LOS.
style.quote_before: In deriving a spread curve for an issuer, the reading uses example data of Eli Lilly (LLY) and Bristol-Myers Squibb (BMS), both A2/A+ rated. Their spread curves are most likely:
style.quote_after: A manager compares two A2/A+ rated pharmaceutical issuers, LLY and BMS, and finds that the market prices slightly greater credit risk for BMS only at the 5-year and near-30-year maturities. Their spread curves are most likely:

style.detail: The stem was de-identified ('a fund', 'the operator of a fund's airport concession') but rationale B still names the operator and the speaker as if the learner had seen them, introducing a proper noun and a job title that appear nowhere in the item: 'AOG is a strong global operator, and a break clause activated in two or three years' time would leave the fund responsible for replacing it' and 'as the head of infrastructure puts it'. In 'before' these names were anchored by the stem itself ('AOG's rumored contract renegotiation'). Substance is intact and the key is unaffected; the rationale simply no longer matches the item's own framing.
style.quote_before: AOG's rumored contract renegotiation is most likely a risk R-SWF should:

style.detail: Rationale A acquires an empirical claim that is not in "before" and that sits awkwardly beside the keyed rationale. Before, rationale A was only "This is not the empirical pattern.", and the substance lived in C: "Categories vary widely across the spectrum from nearly all active to nearly all passive." After, rationale A asserts that category shares cluster at the extremes with "few sitting near a half-and-half division", while after-rationale C still frames the finding as "a spectrum rather than a binary choice". The source material supports a wide range across the spectrum, not a bimodal distribution with a sparse middle. Not fatal: option A ("every category is split evenly between the two") is false on its universal quantifier regardless, so the key and the distractor status are unaffected.
style.quote_before: This is not the empirical pattern.
style.quote_after: Category shares cluster toward one end or the other, with some categories almost entirely active and others almost entirely index-based, and few sitting near a half-and-half division.

style.detail: Rationale C acquired two specific convexity figures that exist nowhere in "before" and nowhere in the rewritten item. "before" rationale C is only: "Incorrect. Convexity enters through Equation 3 - second-order price effects are part of the quantification." "after" rationale C reads: "Convexity enters alongside duration, so second-order price effects are part of the quantification. That is exactly why two portfolios with the same duration but different convexity, 40.229 against 26.5, do not respond identically even to a parallel shift, and why price change is not treated as linear in yield." The numbers 40.229 and 26.5 are unsourced in this item: they are not in the before rationales, not in the reframed stem, and not derivable from anything the learner is given, so the rationale asserts figures from a table the learner cannot open and that this audit cannot verify. The key (B) is still correct and still clearly best, A and C are still false, and each letter carries its prior claim, so the item is not broken - but the added arithmetic is provenance the rewrite did not have and should be dropped or replaced with the generic reasoning the "before" rationale carried.
style.quote_before: Incorrect. Convexity enters through Equation 3 — second-order price effects are part of the quantification.
style.quote_after: two portfolios with the same duration but different convexity, 40.229 against 26.5, do not respond identically even to a parallel shift

style.detail: The reframe rewrote the stem to drop the 'Practice Problem 5' citation and to introduce Pietro and Local Bank, but 'Vogt' now appears exactly once, in option B, with no antecedent anywhere in the item. In 'before', Vogt appeared in both option A ('through Vogt') and option B, and the stem's citation at least pointed at a source where Vogt is identified; the key's option in 'after' no longer mentions Vogt, so the name is left dangling in a distractor alone. Not fatal: the item is still answerable, because A is recognizable as an oversized personal order and B and C are recognizable as truthful disclosures, and the stem supplies the merger/holding-back setup the reasoning needs. Reported as style only.
